q: 1. Permeability of soil varies
options: inversely as square of grain size
explain: From Hazen's/Kozeny-type relations (k = C·D10²), coefficient of permeability is proportional to the square of the effective grain size.

q: 2. The coefficient of permeability is proportional to void ratio (e) as K = 100 D10² i.e., K ∝ D10²
explain: The Kozeny-Carman equation shows permeability is proportional to the function e³/(1+e), which accounts for void ratio's effect on flow paths.

q: 3. The height of capillary rise is maximum in
explain: Capillary rise is inversely proportional to pore/particle size; colloidal (extremely fine) soils have the smallest pores and hence the greatest capillary rise (though very slow).

q: 4. The soil moisture driven off by heat, is called
explain: Hygroscopic (adsorbed) water is held tightly around particles by molecular attraction and is removed only by heating (oven drying), unlike free/gravity water.

q: 5. The capillary rise of water
options: increases as the size of the soil particles increases
decreases as the size of the soil particles decreases
is less in wet soil than in dry soil
explain: Capillary rise is governed by surface tension forces (menisci) at the air-water interface within the pores; hence it fundamentally depends on the responsible surface-tension force, and inversely on pore size.

q: 6. If the specific gravity and voids in soil sample are G and e respectively, the hydraulic gradient i, is
explain: The critical hydraulic gradient (at which quicksand condition occurs) is derived as icr = (G-1)/(1+e), balancing submerged weight against seepage force.

q: 7. Darcy's law is applicable to seepage if a soil is
explain: Darcy's law assumptions include a homogeneous, isotropic, saturated, incompressible medium with laminar flow — all conditions must hold.

q: 8. During seepage through a soil, direction of seepage is always
explain: In a flow net, flow lines (direction of seepage) always cross equipotential lines at right angles, i.e., seepage is perpendicular to equipotential lines.

q: 9. The quantity of seepage of water through soils is proportional to
options: total head loss through the soil
explain: By Darcy's law, q = k·i·A, and since i = head loss/length, seepage quantity is proportional to both permeability and total head loss.

q: 10. The phreatic line in an earth dam may be
explain: The top flow line (phreatic line) of seepage through an earth dam closely approximates a parabola (Casagrande's basic parabola method).

q: 11. The ultimate settlement of a soil is directly proportional to
options: depth of the compressible soil strata
explain: Consolidation settlement Sc = (Cc·H)/(1+e0)·log(...), directly proportional to both the thickness of compressible strata (H) and the compression index (Cc).

q: 12. The neutral stress in a soil mass is
options: stress taken up by the pore water
stress taken up by solid particles
explain: Neutral (pore-water) stress is the portion of total stress carried by water in the pores, as distinguished from effective stress carried by the soil skeleton.

q: 13. The shear strength of soil
options: increases with an increase in the normal stress
is proportional to the cohesion of the soil
is generally known as the strength of the soil
explain: By Coulomb's equation s = c + σ tanφ, shear strength increases with normal stress and cohesion, and is generally regarded as the overall 'strength' of soil — all statements are correct.

q: 14. On wetting, cohesive solid,
explain: Increased moisture reduces inter-particle attraction and increases pore pressure in cohesive soils, thereby decreasing their shear strength.

q: 15. The compression resulting from a long term static load and consequent escape of
explain: Consolidation is precisely the time-dependent compression caused by sustained static load driving pore water out of a saturated fine-grained soil.

q: 16. The reduction in volume of soil due to squeezing out of water from the voids, is termed
explain: The book lists all three terms (primary consolidation, primary compression, primary time effect) as synonymous descriptions of this volume-reduction phenomenon.

q: 17. A sand has e = 0.8 and another clay has e = 1.2, which is more pervious?
explain: Despite its lower void ratio, sand has far larger particles and pore channels than clay, making it much more permeable overall.

q: 18. The ratio of settlement at any time 't' to the final settlement, is known as
explain: Degree of consolidation U = settlement at time t / ultimate (final) settlement, a dimensionless fraction describing consolidation progress.

q: 19. The coefficient of permeability is proportional to void ratio as .............
explain: Permeability is commonly related to void ratio through the expression k ∝ e³/(1+e), based on Kozeny-Carman type relations.

q: 20. The maximum pressure which a soil can carry without shear failure, is called
explain: Safe bearing capacity is the maximum pressure the soil can safely carry without shear failure, incorporating a factor of safety.

q: 21. Which of the following soils has largest permeability?
explain: Gravel has the largest particle size and pore spaces of these soils, giving it the highest permeability.

q: 22. The coefficient grain size of soil (D10) is 0.3 mm, the value of coefficient of permeability as per Hazen is (coefficient of Hazen C = 10) .............
explain: By Hazen's formula, k = C x D10^2 = 10 x (0.3)^2 = 0.9 mm/sec.

q: 23. The permeability of the following soil will be almost zero .............
explain: Fine-grained content in silty/clayey sand fills the pore spaces, drastically reducing permeability compared to clean sands.

q: 24. When a cohesionless soil attains quick condition, it looses
explain: In quicksand condition, effective stress becomes zero due to upward seepage force equalling submerged weight, so the soil loses both its shear strength and bearing capacity.

q: 25. The shearing strength of a cohesion less soil depends upon
explain: For cohesionless (frictional) soils, shear strength s = σ tanφ depends primarily on the normal/confining pressure acting on the failure plane.

q: 26. The property of a soil which is of great importance in finding settlement of structures, is
explain: Consolidation behaviour (rate and magnitude of volume change under load) directly governs long-term settlement calculations for structures.

q: 27. When compared to deformation of thin soil sample because of consolidation, the deformation of thick soil sample will be .............
explain: Because the thick sample has a longer drainage path, its rate of consolidation is slower, so within a given time it shows less deformation than a thin sample (though its eventual total settlement is larger).

q: 28. The time required for the completion of consolidation for a thin soil sample when compared with that of a thick soil sample will be .............
explain: Per the reference key this is left indeterminate; generally, thinner samples with shorter drainage paths consolidate faster than thicker ones.

q: 29. As the value of drainage path increases the time required for consolidation will .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked indeterminate; by consolidation theory (Tv = Cv t/d^2), a longer drainage path normally increases the time required.

q: 30. Which of the following does not happen when compaction is done?
explain: Compaction is intended to increase soil density, which typically increases shear strength; therefore, a decrease in shear strength is what does NOT happen.

q: 31. The change in the thickness of a soil sample may be due to .............
options: expulsion of pore water or pore air from the voids
compression of the soil solid particles
compression of water (or) air in the voids of soil
explain: Volume change in soil during consolidation is primarily due to expulsion of pore water/air from the voids, not compression of the solids themselves.

q: 32. The expression for the discharge (Q) through a flow net for isotropic soils is given by
explain: For an isotropic soil, seepage discharge Q = K·H·(Nf/Nd), where Nf is number of flow channels and Nd is number of potential drops.

q: 33. The degree of consolidation is proportional directly
options: to time and inversely to drainage path
to drainage path and inversely to time
to time and inversely to the square of drainage path
to square of drainage path and inversely to time
explain: The time factor Tv = Cv·t/d² shows degree of consolidation increases with time t and decreases with the square of the drainage path length d.

q: 34. The process of compaction of a soil involves .............
options: expulsion of both pore water and air voids
explain: Compaction (a mechanical process) primarily expels air from the voids; pore water removal instead characterizes consolidation.

q: 35. The most effective method for compacting sand is by using .............
explain: Cohesionless sands compact best under vibratory compaction, which rearranges grains into a denser packing.

q: 36. The earth pressure in the retaining wall is
options: proportional to internal friction of the soil
explain: Lateral earth pressure at any depth p = K·γ·z increases linearly with depth z, so the pressure (intensity) itself is proportional to depth.

q: 37. One dimensional theory of Consolidation of Terzaghi is based on the assumption that
options: excess water is drained out only in the vertical direction
head is applied in one direction
explain: Terzaghi's 1-D consolidation theory assumes constant permeability, purely vertical drainage, and one-directional head/flow — all these assumptions together define the theory.

q: 38. On attaining quick condition, cohesionless soil loses its
explain: In quicksand condition, effective stress vanishes, so the soil loses both its bearing capacity and its shear strength simultaneously.

q: 39. Hygroscopic water can be removed by
explain: Hygroscopic water is held to particle surfaces by molecular attraction, far stronger than gravity, so it can only be removed by heating (oven drying), not by gravity or free flow.

q: 40. The net bearing pressure which can be used for the design of foundations .............
explain: Net allowable bearing pressure is the design value used for proportioning foundations, accounting for both shear failure and settlement limits.

q: 41. The value of net allowable bearing pressure is .............
options: minimum of net safe bearing capacity and net safe settlement pressure
explain: The net allowable bearing pressure is taken as the smaller (more conservative) of the net safe bearing capacity and net safe settlement pressure.

q: 42. The property of a soil which permits water to percolate through it, is called
explain: Permeability is defined as the property of a porous medium (soil) that allows water to flow (percolate) through its voids.

q: 43. The value of mobilized cohesion will be .............
explain: For local/punching shear conditions, mobilized shear parameters are reduced; cohesion is typically taken as 2/3 of the actual cohesion C (Terzaghi's approach).

q: 44. The property of the soil which allows to flow water through the soil is known as
explain: Permeability is the soil property governing the ease with which water can flow through its interconnected voids.

q: 45. The critical exit gradient of the seepage of water in a soil is
explain: The critical hydraulic gradient (at which quicksand condition initiates) equals (G-1)/(1+e), derived by equating seepage force to submerged weight.

q: 46. The compression resulting from long term static load and resulting expulsion of water is known as
explain: Time-dependent volume reduction of saturated soil under sustained load, due to gradual expulsion of pore water, defines consolidation.

q: 47. Absorbed water in soil is
options: the water chemically combined in crystal structure of the soil material
having free movement through the soil by gravity
water absorbed from atmosphere by forces of attraction
explain: Absorbed (structural/adsorbed) water refers to water molecules chemically bound within the crystal lattice of clay minerals, distinct from free or hygroscopic water.

q: 48. The active earth pressure of a soil can be defined as lateral pressure exerted by the soil when
options: the retaining wall tends to move away from the back fill
wall moves relative to the back fill
explain: Active earth pressure develops when the wall yields/moves away from the backfill, allowing the soil to expand and mobilize its shear strength to a minimum pressure state.

q: 49. The lateral earth pressure of the soil moves towards the retaining wall indicates
explain: When the soil mass itself tends to move toward (push against) the wall while the wall yields away, this describes the active earth pressure condition.

q: 50. Primary consolidation of soil is due to the expulsion of .............
explain: Primary consolidation results mainly from the gradual expulsion of free (absorbed) pore water from the soil under load.
